title: Routing simulation lab notebook: latency/cost/reliability tradeoffs
content:
Purpose:
This is a working lab notebook for experimental routing policies and small-scale simulations that explore the tradeoffs between latency, unit cost, and cross-region reliability. The goal is to capture quick hypotheses, scenario setups, metric definitions, and lightweight decision logic we can iterate on before formalizing a control-plane policy DSL proposal.

Audience:
Platform engineers, SREs, and applied ML who will review simulation outcomes and propose productionizable policy components. Not an exhaustive design doc — think: experiments + heuristics + TODOs.

Context and motivation:
- We frequently need to route inference requests across: local-region hosted clusters (low latency, higher cost), cheaper cold capacity (lower priority, lower cost), and cross-region fallback pools (higher latency, high reliability when local is down).
- Simple static priority lists underperform when workload mixes short-chat p99 latency SLAs and background batch embeddings; we want a policy that is signal-driven, auditable, and easy to simulate.

Key signals considered (captured in sims):
- latency_estimate_ms (95th predicted latency for route under current load)
- unit_cost_usd_per_1k_tokens (model + infra cost estimate)
- success_rate_1m (fraction of successful responses last minute)
- kv_cache_hit_rate (prefix caching helps short sessions)
- request_priority (user defined: interactive | background | realtime-critical)

Metric definitions (sim outputs):
- SLA_violation_rate: fraction of interactive requests with latency > 150ms (configurable per sim)
- cost_per_100k_tokens: simulated billing estimate for the workload mix
- observed_uptime: percent time at least one route returns before timeout
- regret_index: weighted sum: 3*SLA_violation_rate + 1*(cost_norm) + 2*(1 - observed_uptime) — used for quick comparatives in notebooks

Simulation scenarios (short):
1) Morning surge (75% interactive short chats, spiky qps): test batching effects and tiny tails.
2) Long-running embeddings pipeline (background, can tolerate 2x latency): test cheap pool & queuing.
3) Region outage (simulate local region limp mode): test multi-region fallback persistence and cost blowup.
4) Mixed reliability-sensitive customers (pinning + canary rollouts): test route pinning behavior and automatic fallback.

Config snippets (simple policy pseudocode used in sims):
- score(route) = alpha * normalized(latency_estimate_ms) + beta * normalized(unit_cost) - gamma * normalized(success_rate)
- route_select(request) = argmin_route { score(route) subject to route.capacities >= request.batch_size and route.slo_eligible(request) }
- slo_eligible: for request.priority == 'realtime-critical' only routes with latency_estimate_ms_p50 < target_lat_ms are allowed; background requests can pick cheapest route with success_rate > 0.95

Example policy variants we tried (notes):
- Latency-first: alpha=0.7, beta=0.2, gamma=0.1 -> very few SLA violations but cost high.
- Cost-first with reliability guard: alpha=0.2, beta=0.6, gamma=0.2 -> cost down, but p99 spikes during surges.
- Adaptive hysteresis: change alpha per-minute based on recent SLA_violation_rate; reduces oscillation during transient overloads.

Decision tree (ascii) used to evaluate a single request at runtime in sims:

  [start] request arrives (priority, batch_size, region_pref)
       |
       v
  Is region_pref pinned? -- yes --> try pinned pool --> if success return, else fallthrough to fallback step
       |no
       v
  Is request.priority == realtime-critical? -- yes --> shortlist routes where latency_estimate_p50 < target_lat_ms and success_rate > 0.995
       |                               |
       |                               v (if empty) -> try local high-priority pool with timeout short; if fail, escalate to cross-region with tracing tag
       v
  For non-critical: compute score(route) and pick argmin subject to success_rate>0.9
       |
       v
  If picked_route.load_estimate + batch_size > route.capacity_soft_limit -> consider secondary cheaper pool with queuing or apply immediate fallback to next route (hysteresis window 30s)

Operational heuristics (less formal, from lab lessons):
- Keep reliability thresholds conservative in simulations (0.99+) for production candidates; small improvements in cost often amplify outage risk during correlated failures.
- Use prefix-KV cache signal to short-circuit latency-first policies (if kv_cache_hit_rate > 0.6 prefer cached route even if cost slightly higher).
- For canary traffic, bias scores toward local region first but tag traces with route decision reasons for later audit.
- Enforce a rate-limited promo to cheaper pools to avoid sudden cold-start storms; simulate ramp-up windows (1–5 minutes) for cold pools.

Simulation implementation details (notes to engineers):
- Event-driven simulator with: request generator, route model (latency distribution, cost, capacity), caching layer, and simple network flakiness model (5 classes of failure modes).
- Use synthetic traces derived from prod token/time histograms (sampled) rather than IID Poisson; burstiness matters more than mean QPS.
- Capture per-route time-series (1s granularity) for latency P50/P95/P99, error counts, and token costs.

Open questions (to decide before formal policy doc):
- What degree of policy explainability/auditability do we require? Should every decision produce a structured reason (route_id, score_components)? Pros: debugging and customer reports. Cons: slightly larger trace payloads and storage.
- Do we bake in per-customer routing budgets (e.g., limit background traffic to cheap pools up to X tokens/day) into the control plane? How to surface in billing?
- Rollout controls: can we declaratively express "prefer cheaper pool when cost_delta < 5% and SLA_violation_rate < 0.1%"? Need DSL semantics for nested boolean + threshold guards.

Experiment outcomes summary (very rough):
- Latency-first variant: SLA_violation_rate ~0.4% in surge sim, cost_per_100k_tokens ~ $410.
- Cost-first variant w/ reliability guard: SLA_violation_rate ~1.8% in surge sim, cost ~ $290.
- Adaptive hysteresis: SLA_violation_rate ~0.8%, cost ~ $330; much less oscillation in route selection than cost-first.

Next steps / action items:
- (Priya) Re-run region outage sims with longer tail latencies (simulate DVFS-induced slowdowns) and capture sensitivity. Due: 2024-02-28.
- (Diego) Add structured decision-reason output to simulator traces (route_score components). Important for audit. Due: 2024-02-24.
- (Evan) Prototype small DSL snippet in repo (github.com/redwood-inference/routing-dsl) and wire up to sim harness. Due: 2024-03-05.
- (Anika) Draft short proposal for control-plane API surface: evaluate/predict/choose verbs + reason object + fallback policies. Due: 2024-03-12.

Loose ends / notes to self:
- Think about integrating with Rollouts: canary rules should map to the same scoring function but with higher bias to new model versions.
- Add a "safety multiplier" for models under training/test to avoid early full-traffic routing.
- Document storage cost implications of storing per-request reason payloads; consider sampler.

Appendix: small example "reason" payload we log in sims (flattened key=value lines for prototype):
- request_id=abc123 | chosen_route=r-us-east-2-high | score=0.423 | latency_comp=0.31 | cost_comp=0.09 | reliability_comp=0.02 | cache_hit=false | fallback_attempts=0

Meeting notes (quick):
- 2024-01-18: discussed hysteresis windows; consensus: 30s initial, can tune to 2x typical route adjustment latency.
- 2024-02-05: SRE asked for explicit grace period for pinned routes (avoid evicting pinned traffic immediately during capacity churn).

If you run sims, drop results as CSVs to the linked repo path and ping #eng-platform for review. The sim harness is intentionally intentionally small so we can iterate fast.

End of notebook.
